User: Can you summarize the main reasons for the slump in Indiana's basketball teams, including the Pacers, Hoosiers, and Butler?: IU, Butler and Pacers are in freefall at same time, for same reason.
Pacers, Hoosiers, Butler … it's hard times for a populace that puts so much of itself into its basketball teams, and is getting so little in return.
INDIANAPOLIS – Hard to be happy around here this winter, isn’t it? No sun. Too damn cold. Plus we have another reason: We’re living in a basketball state with some seriously bad basketball.
It’s not just Butler’s effort. It’s the Pacers and Hoosiers, who also suffered ugly losses Wednesday night, and whose coaches have made it clear that their teams, same as Jordan was saying of Butler, are lacking something beyond talent. Something closer to effort.
Listen to Pacers coach Nate McMillan: “It’s just low energy right now. We've kind of lost our way here and we've got to find it ... We got to get more energy in the game."
More energy? That’s code for “more effort.” Those are fighting words, or should be, if his team – if any of these teams – have any fight left.
What’s happening here? Let me take a swing at this.
When their mind’s right, the Pacers have shown this season they can win without Victor Oladipo. They were 7-4 in games without him before he suffered a torn quadriceps tendon early against the Toronto Raptors on Jan. 23, and as an example of how this team can play when its mind is right: The Pacers won that game anyway.
And the Pacers aren’t responding well. McMillan keeps saying the same thing: The Pacers need to stop focusing on who’s gone, and focus on who’s here. Clearly that’s easier to do when it's temporary, holding down the fort for a game or two as opposed to facing three months without your singular star and emotional heartbeat.
Beyond the psychological shock, losing Oladipo underscores the biggest issue with this team in an evolving NBA: Two of the Pacers’ best three players are centers, which means they rarely play together, in an era where perimeter scoring and playmaking is at a premium.
And when the only one of those three who plays the perimeter, Oladipo, goes out? Well, look: Myles Turner and Domantas Sabonis are fabulous young talents, they really are. But the Pacers need more guards. They have some young ones in Aaron Holiday and Edmond Sumner who will get more minutes. They’d better be good and ready.
And bring this team more effort, huh?
Archie Miller got tough. He called out his players after the loss to Nebraska. I was there, and it was shocking. And it didn’t work.
Will the soft touch work? Not sure it fits Miller’s style, to be honest. He’s a no-nonsense guy, a grinder, a winner as a player despite his small size, and a winner as a coach (at Dayton) by taking a roster full of overlooked recruits and turning them into something mean, something ferocious.
The Hoosiers have a better roster than Dayton ever had. But they’re not mean. Not ferocious. Archie's teams at Dayton would have eaten this IU team for lunch, and asked for another meal two hours later.
At Rutgers, where the Knights reeled off 22 consecutive points, the Hoosiers looked, frankly, soft. At Purdue they looked, frankly, scared.
A quick word about Miller: IU fans are freaking out, some of them anyway – OK, a lot of them – and wondering if Miller was the wrong guy to replace Tom Crean. And I’m telling you it’s way too soon to say that. It’s way too soon even to wonder that.
Here’s what happens when a fan base this large and passionate freaks out: It makes things so much harder on the coach, on the players, on the program. A fan base like Indiana’s, as big as it is, can be the wind in its team’s sails … or its face.
Am I blaming you, IU fans, for what has happened here? Not at all. Not any. But going forward, there is a choice to be made, and this team – as well as potential recruits – will be watching to see your decision.
Watch the players on the court, on the bench. Watch the way they interact, or in the case of Butler, the way they don’t.
The Bulldogs had no enthusiasm against Marquette, not for the game, not for each other. LaVall Jordan was blaming himself for that afterward, and up to a point, he’s right. Players can be an extension of their coach, and Jordan is cerebral. He’s a calm, quiet man, and he has a team that is too calm, too quiet. Can Jordan change the emotional makeup of his team? Can he become more like Archie, while Archie is trying to become more like LaVall?
On the Butler side, I saw pure passion one time all night Wednesday, and it was more than an hour after the game when I was leaving the Hinkle media room and heard a ball bouncing on the court. I walked to the tunnel and saw him: senior Paul Jorgensen sprinting around the court, getting up shots, working on a game that has indeed gone south. After averaging 17.2 points on 43.1-percent 3-point shooting through nine games, Jorgensen has dipped to 7.5 ppg on 34.6-percent shooting in the last 13.
Now, pay attention please: Am I blaming Paul Jorgensen for the Bulldogs’ slide from 7-2 to 12-10, and 3-6 in the Big East? Not at all. Not any. I’m bringing him up to show you what passion looks like, what caring looks like, and his was the only passion or care I saw Wednesday night. And it came an hour after the gym had emptied out.
The problems facing Butler are different from those facing the Pacers and Hoosiers, but the fixes are mostly the same: The players need to care more. The coaches need to make that happen. It’s not on somebody – it’s on everybody.
Meanwhile, in our basketball state with some really bad basketball, there’s always Purdue.
And doesn’t that seem to be true? There’s always Purdue.

What’s happening here? Let me take a swing at this.

User: What is placemaking, and how can it enhance the character and identity of a neighborhood or district?
Assistant: Placemaking is a community-based process that involves the planning, design, and implementation of public spaces to create vibrant, accessible, and inviting places. It is a collaborative effort that involves neighborhood residents, business owners, community organizations, and local government officials to create public spaces that reflect the unique character and identity of a neighborhood or district.

Through placemaking, communities can enhance the character of their neighborhood and improve the quality of life for residents. Placemaking can help to create more attractive and functional public spaces, such as parks, streetscapes, and public squares, that encourage social interaction, support local businesses, and create a sense of place.

Placemaking can also help to preserve the historical, cultural, and architectural heritage of a neighborhood, and promote sustainable development practices. By engaging local communities in the planning and design process, placemaking can build a sense of ownership and pride among residents, which can lead to a more resilient and sustainable community in the long run.

Overall, placemaking is an important tool for enhancing the character and identity of a neighborhood or district, and can help to create vibrant, healthy, and sustainable communities that are enjoyable places to live, work, and play.
User: That sounds really interesting! Can you give me an example of a successful placemaking project?
Assistant: Sure, here's an example of a successful placemaking project:

The High Line in New York City is a beautiful example of placemaking. The High Line is a 1.45-mile-long elevated park that was created from an abandoned railway track on the west side of Manhattan. Community members, local businesses, and city officials worked together to transform the abandoned track into a beautiful park that provides a unique and beautiful public space for New York residents and visitors alike.

The High Line is a great example of how placemaking can help to enhance the character and identity of a neighborhood or district. It has become a destination for both tourists and locals alike, and has helped to attract new businesses to the area. Since it opened, property values in the area have risen, and the park has been credited with creating a sense of community and pride among local residents.

Overall, the High Line shows how effective placemaking can be in creating new public spaces that enhance the character and identity of a neighborhood or district, and can help to promote economic development and social connections.

2. "The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces" by William H. Whyte - This classic book is based on a study of public spaces in New York City and provides insights into the design and use of successful public spaces. It includes observations on human behavior, as well as recommendations for designing successful public spaces.

3. "Placemaking and the Future of Cities" by Charles R. Wolfe - This book examines the role of placemaking in creating vibrant and sustainable cities. It explores the relationship between urban design, community engagement, and economic development, and provides case studies of successful placemaking efforts.

4. "Tactical Urbanism" by Mike Lydon and Anthony Garcia - This book focuses on small-scale, quick, and low-cost interventions that can be used to improve public spaces. It provides practical advice on how to implement these tactics and includes case studies from around the world.

There are also many websites and organizations focused on placemaking, including Project for Public Spaces and The Placemaking Leadership Council, which offer a wealth of resources and information on this important topic.

With love and admiration for everything that you are,

Sincerely,

You could invite residents to submit their own artwork ideas or have a community art project where everyone contributes. 3. 2. Garden games: Set up a few garden games like cornhole, croquet, or ladder toss, that people can play while enjoying the garden's scenery.

3. Group planting session: Invite everyone to plant a small herb or flower together in a designated area of the garden. Encourage people to share their stories or experiences of gardening.

6. Live music performance: Provide acoustic live music that people can enjoy while they're relaxing in the garden.

These are just a few examples, but the sky's the limit for activities you could organize. Mix and match activities to suit the audience and make sure everyone has plenty of fun!

User: Can you provide more information on the benefits of walkability in real estate and how it affects home prices?: Berkeley News, Dining Out, East Bay Neighborhoods, Good Times!, Home Buyers, Homebuyers, Interesting Facts, Lifestyle, Oakland News, Real Estate News, The Scoop!
Remember when homes in the Berkeley and Oakland hills commanded premium prices and multiple offers because of their quiet suburban appeal and spectacular Bay and City views? Well, a new era of buyers have been flipping that East Bay home sales trend on its head. Now the flats are where it’s at, in part, because they are so walkable.
Hot neighborhoods include Bushrod, Temescal and Rockridge – all easy walks to BART stations, bus stops, schools and booming commercial districts with farm-to-table dining, bookstores, craft brew pubs, funky and upscale shops, gourmet markets and children’s stores.
Younger people moving from The City want a more urban feel and amenities without the parking headaches. Retired baby boomers don’t want to drive and have time to enjoy urban amenities. Easy access to the arts and theater in downtown Berkeley is a big draw.
Nationally, more than half of millennials and 46 percent of boomers prefer walkable communities, according to a survey by the American Planning Association.
Cafes and shops along College Avenue are within easy walking distance for Rockridge residents.
Where else is it hot to be flat?
Bushrod: This north Oakland neighborhood was named the country’s hottest housing market by Redfin in January because of peak buyer interest. Bushrod’s charm includes its namesake park and easy access to Ashby and MacArthur BART stations.
Northbrae: North Berkeley’s most BARTable neighborhood sits between Berkeley’s famous “Gourmet Ghetto” and the Solano Avenue shops. But with Monterey Market and Gioa Pizza, residents don’t even have to go that far.
Temescal: One of Oakland’s oldest neighborhoods, Temescal is centered on Telegraph Avenue. Oakland’s vibrant neighborhood draws hipsters and young families to its inspiring restaurants, nearby shops, cafes and popular Farmers’ Market.
El Cerrito: More families are considering this part of Contra Costa County for the conveniences, including El Cerrito shopping plaza, a BART station, the Ohlone Greenway, restaurants and a revitalized portion of San Pablo Avenue.
Westbrae: The Berkeley neighborhood has easy access to Gilman Street for shopping and dining (the highly acclaimed Lalime’s and Westbrae Biergarten are here). It’s home to strollers and coffee seekers in the mornings and craft beer aficionados in the afternoons. Westbrae also boasts a beautiful community garden and the Ohlone Greenway.
If you live in the flats and are considering selling, now is the obviously time for East Bay home sales. Redfin studied how much walkability is worth when buying or selling a home and found that one Walk Score point can increase the price of a home by an average of $3,250 or 0.9 percent.
That holds true elsewhere in East Bay home sales, even though walkability is harder to come by on the other side of the Caldecott Tunnel. Expect to sell at a higher price per square foot in foot-friendly neighborhoods in Lafayette (the Trail area and parts of Happy Valley), Walnut Creek (Saranap and Parkmead) and Danville (Westside).
Excerpts and Images for this post courtesy of Abio Properties Blog.

By incorporating these tips, you can improve the walkability of your neighborhood and increase the value of your home.

Remember when homes in the Berkeley and Oakland hills commanded premium prices and multiple offers because of their quiet suburban appeal and spectacular Bay and City views? Well, a new era of buyers have been flipping that East Bay home sales trend on its head. Now the flats are where it’s at, in part, because they are so walkable.
Hot neighborhoods include Bushrod, Temescal and Rockridge – all easy walks to BART stations, bus stops, schools and booming commercial districts with farm-to-table dining, bookstores, craft brew pubs, funky and upscale shops, gourmet markets and children’s stores.
Younger people moving from The City want a more urban feel and amenities without the parking headaches. Retired baby boomers don’t want to drive and have time to enjoy urban amenities. Easy access to the arts and theater in downtown Berkeley is a big draw.
Nationally, more than half of millennials and 46 percent of boomers prefer walkable communities, according to a survey by the American Planning Association.
Cafes and shops along College Avenue are within easy walking distance for Rockridge residents.
Where else is it hot to be flat?
Bushrod: This north Oakland neighborhood was named the country’s hottest housing market by Redfin in January because of peak buyer interest. Bushrod’s charm includes its namesake park and easy access to Ashby and MacArthur BART stations.
Northbrae: North Berkeley’s most BARTable neighborhood sits between Berkeley’s famous “Gourmet Ghetto” and the Solano Avenue shops. But with Monterey Market and Gioa Pizza, residents don’t even have to go that far.
Temescal: One of Oakland’s oldest neighborhoods, Temescal is centered on Telegraph Avenue. Oakland’s vibrant neighborhood draws hipsters and young families to its inspiring restaurants, nearby shops, cafes and popular Farmers’ Market.
El Cerrito: More families are considering this part of Contra Costa County for the conveniences, including El Cerrito shopping plaza, a BART station, the Ohlone Greenway, restaurants and a revitalized portion of San Pablo Avenue.
Westbrae: The Berkeley neighborhood has easy access to Gilman Street for shopping and dining (the highly acclaimed Lalime’s and Westbrae Biergarten are here). It’s home to strollers and coffee seekers in the mornings and craft beer aficionados in the afternoons. Westbrae also boasts a beautiful community garden and the Ohlone Greenway.
If you live in the flats and are considering selling, now is the obviously time for East Bay home sales. Redfin studied how much walkability is worth when buying or selling a home and found that one Walk Score point can increase the price of a home by an average of $3,250 or 0.9 percent.
That holds true elsewhere in East Bay home sales, even though walkability is harder to come by on the other side of the Caldecott Tunnel. Expect to sell at a higher price per square foot in foot-friendly neighborhoods in Lafayette (the Trail area and parts of Happy Valley), Walnut Creek (Saranap and Parkmead) and Danville (Westside).

Assistant: Oh, you liked Jeepers Creepers? I'm glad to hear that.
User: Can you recommend me another movie?
Assistant: Sure, how about What's Happening!!: Season 1? It has received positive reviews.
User: That sounds interesting. Can you tell me more about it?
Assistant: What's Happening!!: Season 1 is an underrated sitcom from the seventies. It revolves around three African American friends from the Watts neighborhood in Los Angeles. The first season is considered the best, especially with Mabel King playing Mama. It tackles various issues with humor and sensitivity.
User: Sounds good. I'll give it a try.
Assistant: Great! Is there anything else I can recommend to you?
User: No, thank you. I appreciate your help.
Assistant: You're welcome! If you have any other questions in the future, feel free to ask. Have a great day!
User: Hi there! I really enjoyed reading "Give Me Something". It had a great premise and unexpected twists. I would definitely recommend it. (Review: I really enjoyed the premise of the book. The author did a fantastic job of setting up a character that's unlikable, but made us like her anyway. I especially liked that there were twists and turns I didn't see coming. It was a fun read and I'd definitely check out other stuff by Lee.)
Assistant: I'm glad to hear that you enjoyed "Give Me Something"! If you're interested, I can recommend another book you might like. How about "The Good Neighbor"? (Review: The Good Neighbor by A. J. Banner opens with a scene that left me breathless and promised a page-turner -- a promise kept, as I had trouble putting it down. Sarah McDonald settles in to Shadow Cove, Washington, with her new (and handsome) husband, Johnny. All is well until a tragedy occurs, leaving Sarah vulnerable and uncertain. As the mystery deepens, so do her self-doubts, leaving her unable to know whom to trust. Sarah's unease increases throughout the story, and so does the reader's. What I appreciate most about A. J. Banner's writing is her ability to convey the world of Shadow Cove so we can inhabit it fully. I can see the neighborhood and the people who inhabit it. Her characters are rich and distinct from each other. Jessie and Mia, one a teen and the other a young child, both touched my heart, and the other characters are richly layered. This allows Banner to keep us guessing with the twists and turns. While The Good Neighbor is a riveting story, its greatest strength is its ability to connect emotionally with the reader. It's fast-paced and will appeal to those who like plot-driven stories, but I felt invested in several of these characters, as though I knew them, and that's what I liked best.)
User: Actually, I didn't enjoy "The Good Neighbor". The writing style felt flat and the lack of research into certain aspects bothered me. (Review: The writing wasn't really what I would consider good. It was kind of flat, boring--shallow. Very much: The cat went in. The cat went out. I watched. Which in itself isn't unforgivable. Sometimes, that works well for a thriller. What was the real killer for me was the lack of research into basically everything. If you're going to write about a murder investigation, you need to understand how they work. If you're going to give a character a specific job, you need to understand what they do in the course of their work and when you mention rare diseases, you also need to understand how those work. A couple hours of research would've fixed this. I also had a problem with the characterization of pretty much every female character. They were all one-dimensional, like props for the story and for the protag's insecurities. This book seemed to be a hyper manifestation of every negative female stereotype.)
Assistant: I understand your concerns about "The Good Neighbor". In that case, let me recommend another book that you might like - "Blood Business: Crime Stories From This World And Beyond". It's a collection of creepy and spine-chilling stories that will stay with you long after reading. (Review: Well, well, well, this book is not for the faint of heart! If you want to read a creepy and often stomach-churning set of stories, this is absolutely your best choice. One of my favorite stories in here was "Girls Gone Wild" (not what you think it's about) and it's a great way of someone getting their "just desserts" so to speak with a nifty twist at the end. The other stories were just spine-chilling and creepy and not the kind of thing you want to read before a meal (or before bed), I'd say. I thought at first these would be more along the lines of crime solving, like murder mysteries, but these stories are a tad more violent than that. It's the type of stories that will stay with you long after they are over. I'm very much into short story collections like this because each story is uniquely told all under the same umbrella of "crime.")
User: That sounds intriguing! I'll give "Blood Business: Crime Stories From This World And Beyond" a try. Thanks for the recommendation!
Assistant: You're welcome! If you need any more book recommendations, feel free to ask. Happy reading!
User: Thank you so much for your help. I appreciate it!
Assistant: It was my pleasure. Have a great day and happy reading!

User: Okay, I think I'll try that. Thanks for the suggestion.
Assistant: You're welcome. Remember, you don't have to face any difficult memories or emotions alone. I'm here to support you.
User: I appreciate that. I think I'm starting to realize that my childhood was affected by the war. I was so young when it happened, but it had a profound impact on my life.
Assistant: I'm so sorry to hear that you experienced the war as a child. That must have been incredibly difficult and scary for you. Can you tell me more about what you remember from that time?
User: Yeah...I remember the sounds of gunfire and explosions, the smell of smoke and fear. I remember having to hide in our basement for hours, not knowing if we'd be safe.
Assistant: Those must have been incredibly traumatic experiences. It's no wonder that they've stayed with you all these years. Have you talked to anyone about your experiences during the war?
User: No, not really. I've tried to push it to the back of my mind, but lately, it's been coming back up.
Assistant: It's never too late to seek help and support. Talking to a therapist or counselor can be really helpful in processing your emotions and experiences. Would you like some resources on how to get started?

Assistant: I'm here to listen and help if I can. Can you tell me more about what's been going on and how you've been feeling?

Assistant: It sounds like you're experiencing some strong emotional responses to certain triggers. Have you noticed any patterns or common themes in what's triggering these reactions?
User: Yeah, I guess so. It's usually things that remind me of past experiences that were traumatic or stressful.
Assistant: I see. It can be really tough to deal with the aftermath of traumatic experiences. Have you talked to anyone about what you're going through, like a therapist or counselor?
User: Yeah, I've been seeing a therapist. They've been trying to help me work through some of this stuff, but it's just really hard.
Assistant: That's great that you're seeking help and support. It takes a lot of courage to face these kinds of challenges head-on. Can you tell me more about what your therapist has been saying or what you've been working on in your sessions?
User: We've been talking about emotional regulation and how I can better manage my emotions when I get triggered. But to be honest, it's just really hard for me to control my emotions sometimes.
Assistant: Emotional regulation can be a really tough skill to develop, especially when you've experienced trauma. But it's great that you're working on it. Have you noticed any small successes or improvements in your ability to manage your emotions?
User: Yeah, I guess so. Some days are better than others. But recently, my therapist told me that I have complex post-traumatic stress disorder, or CPTSD. I'm still trying to wrap my head around what that means.

User: Yeah, that makes sense. I've definitely experienced some repeated trauma in my life, and it feels like it's had a lasting impact on me.

User: Yeah, we've talked about some different things, like mindfulness and grounding techniques. But it's hard for me to remember to use them when I'm in the middle of a crisis.

Assistant: There was a time in my life when I felt lost and unsure of myself. It all started after I graduated from college and was looking for a job. I thought that with my degree, I would be able to secure a good job almost immediately. However, things didn't work out as I expected.

I applied to several jobs, but I didn't get any response. I started doubting my abilities and questioning my decisions. I thought that maybe I had made the wrong choices in the past, and that's why I was not successful. I became very anxious and depressed. I didn't know what to do with my life.

During that time, I isolated myself from my loved ones. I stopped attending social events and stopped talking to my friends. I would spend my days in my room, sleeping and browsing the internet. I was lost, and I didn't see a way out.

However, I realized that I couldn't keep living like that. I needed to do something to overcome my feelings of helplessness and hopelessness. So, I decided to seek help. I went to see a therapist, and I also started attending support groups for people who were experiencing what I was going through.

Speaking to the therapist and other people who were in the same situation as me helped me to understand that I was not alone. I learned that many people go through times when they feel lost and unsure of themselves. I also learned that the most important thing was to keep moving forward, even if it's just a little step at a time.

Another thing I learned was the importance of self-care. I started to take care of myself better. I would exercise, eat healthy, and meditate. I also started to engage in activities that I enjoyed, such as reading and writing.

Eventually, I did find a job that I enjoyed, and I started to feel better about myself. Looking back, I realized that the experience taught me a lot about resilience and the importance of seeking help when necessary. I learned that things can get better, even when they seem hopeless.

I know that my behavior hurt those around me, but I just couldn't bring myself to interact with them at the time. I was afraid that if I spoke to them, they would see me as a failure or judge me for my situation. However, as I mentioned earlier, seeking help through a therapist and support groups played a significant role in helping me to cope with the feelings of rejection. Talking to people who were going through similar situations helped me to feel less alone and more supported. Working with a therapist helped me to understand that my feelings of helplessness were common and that it was okay to ask for support from my loved ones. It prompted me to reach out to my family and friends to share my struggles and ask for their help, advice, and encouragement. Over time, I began to rebuild the relationships that I had neglected. By speaking to them and sharing what I was going through, I realized that they were there for me and that they wanted to support me. With their love and help, I found the strength to face my challenges and persevere through my difficulties. Looking back, I am grateful for the people in my life who helped me during this time, and I have learned that I can't go through tough times alone. It gave us an opportunity to connect with others who were in a similar situation and to learn from their successes and challenges. The facilitator of the group also offered workshops on topics such as networking, resume writing, and interviewing skills. These workshops were helpful in showing us how we could improve our job hunting skills and giving us practical tools to use in our job search. In addition to the workshops and discussion sessions, the group also provided role-playing activities that helped us practice job interviews and networking tips. We also had guest speakers who gave us insights into industry secrets and what employers were looking for in a candidate. Being a part of the support group helped me to gain a sense of community and belonging with people who were all facing similar struggles. Seeing how others were coping with their situations was inspiring and gave me hope. I was able to share my experiences with them and learn some helpful tips to handle difficult job interviews or rejection letters. The group provided a safe space for me to pour out my emotions and feelings of helplessness without feeling judged. By attending the group meetings regularly, I was able to build resilience and regain my confidence in my abilities. Overall, participating in support groups was an important part of my recovery process, and I would definitely recommend it to others who are feeling lost, unsure, or struggling with their challenges.

I am my father’s blue eyes.
I am my mother’s weak mind.
Boys playing footy on the footy field.
Girls dancing in the ballroom.
The beating heart of a new born child.
The traffic on busy roads.
The chips and gravy in my mouth.
The water I drink when my mouth gets dry.
The milk that fuels my body.
The words my mother once said to me.
The reassurance that they love me.
The times I spent with my other family.
The feeling of sadness when I missed them.
I am like a butterfly, wrapped up in a cacoon waiting to break free.
I am the warrior of the future.
I am the maths brains of my father.
Apples crunching in my mouth.
The sweat taste of cake.
And all the times I almost died.
And about what would be different if I died.
I am the deep thinker of the future.
I am the Unique Woman of the future.
This is a personal poem about me.
I am a child of a broken home.
I am the long hair from my mother.
I am the eyes of my father.
Trains coming through the small town.
The drama in the schoolyard.
The sparkling stars shining bright.
The whispers of the children.
Names I do not appreciate.
Teachers telling us what to do.
The loneliness when I sit by myself.
The warm cheesy taste of margarita pizza.
The times when I feel proud of myself.
The happy sleepovers and birthday party’s growing up.
The big smiles from my brothers and sisters.
The time when I met my dad.
What would have happened if I stayed in Melbourne?
How I miss my younger siblings.
What I could become when I’m older.
I am like a buzzing bee working hard. Bees are under appreciated and feared by others.
I wrote this poem about myself. I thought some paarts were hard because I don't really know myself.
I am all things of my past.
I am my mother’s delicacy.
I am my father’s growth.
The happiness of people around me.
The flashes of a camera.
The screams of people around me.
The notes changing on a Clarinet.
The spine cracking as I read a book.
The softness of my kitten.
The pain when I get knocked down.
The saltiness when I accidently take a gulp of the ocean.
The sourness of my dad’s bread.
When I met my favourite artist.
The pain when I broke my arm.
When I had a tea party with my friend from Melbourne.
A frog in my sandpit.
I think about where I’ll be in 20 years.
I think about being tumbled about in the waves.
I think my life would have been like if I stayed in Melbourne.
I think about life after death.
I think about leaving Wycheproof.
I am like a Mandala, lots of work done on me but only to have it wiped away.
I am the success of the future.
This is a poem about myself. I actually found it easy to write.
I am my father’s curls.
I am my mother’s build.
Netballs or tennis balls being launched down the court.
Naughty brothers fighting in the lounge room.
Gymnasts or acrobats flying through the air.
The wind whistling in my ears.
The strings on my guitar being strummed to the rhythm.
The cheering when I do something well.
The stabbing pain of something hurting.
The relief when everything goes well.
The sweetness of candy when it enters my mouth.
The memories of fun and games with my family.
The secrets being shared with my friends.
The moments that make me proud when I finally get the move right.
I am all the things that make me happy.
Acing the opponent in a game of tennis.
Swinging on the bars in gymnastics.
Seeing everyone happy and smiling.
Watching the birds in the sky or the clouds moving slowly.
I am like a shooting star flying and unstoppable.
I am a star of a future.

Assistant: Yes, here are some tips on how to deal with negative thoughts and emotions while training for ultra distances:

1. Practice positive self-talk: When negative thoughts come to mind, replace them with positive affirmations. Focus on the present moment and think about what you're doing well.

2. Break the distance down into smaller parts: Rather than focusing on how far you have to go, focus on the next mile or even the next step. Celebrate small victories along the way.

3. Find a training partner: Having someone to train with can help keep you accountable and provide motivation and support.

4. Set realistic goals: Goal-setting is important, but make sure your goals are achievable and realistic to avoid feeling discouraged.

5. Focus on the process, not just the outcome: Remember that progress is more important than perfection. Enjoy the journey and the improvements you make along the way.

6. Practice self-care: Take good care of your physical and emotional health through good nutrition, adequate rest, stress management, and self-compassion.

7. Seek support: Talk to friends or other runners who may have experienced similar feelings or seek guidance from a mental health professional if needed. Remember that seeking help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

5. Be flexible: You don't have to stick to a rigid training plan. Allow yourself the freedom to adjust your workouts when unexpected events or important life events arise.
